section.title: Instantaneous rate of change
section.p: Average velocity spans an interval; instantaneous velocity describes a single moment. To avoid the forbidden division by zero (\frac{0}{0}), we compute the average rate over a non-zero interval h and take the limit as h\to 0.

statement.p: Let s(t)=t^2 meters after t seconds. The average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is
As h\to 0, the average velocity approaches 4\text{ m/s}, which is the instantaneous velocity at t=2.

subsection.title: Tangent slope
subsection.p: Geometrically, f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of y=f(x) at (a, f(a)). The equation of this tangent line is

figure.caption: Secant slopes approach the tangent slope as the second point approaches the first.
A tangent line can cross the curve. Tangency is defined by limiting slope, not by whether the line touches or crosses.

subsection.title: The derivative as a limit
subsection.p: The derivative is defined through three nested concepts:

li.p: The difference quotient \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is an average rate of change over an interval.
The limit h\to 0 shrinks the interval toward the single point a.
The resulting limit f'(a) is the instantaneous rate of change.

example.title: Failure of differentiability at a sharp corner

statement.p: Let f(x)=|x|. At a=0, the difference quotient is \frac{|h|}{h}.
As h\to 0^+, \frac{|h|}{h} = 1, while as h\to 0^-, \frac{|h|}{h} = -1. Because the one-sided limits disagree, f'(0) does not exist.

figure.caption: At a corner, the left and right limiting slopes disagree, so no derivative exists.

subsection.p: By letting the point a vary across the domain, we transition from calculating slopes at isolated points to studying the derivative as an entirely new function.
